article.title: From Fragmentation to Collapse: How Shared Structures Lose Legitimacy and Become Captured
article.summary: Failure of a shared structure is often a sequence rather than one break: local realities separate, legitimacy erodes, common coordination becomes captured by partial interests, and the structure eventually loses the ability to keep multiple runtimes moving together.

blocks.text: Failure of a shared structure is often a sequence rather than one break: local realities separate, legitimacy erodes, common coordination becomes captured by partial interests, and the structure eventually loses the ability to keep multiple runtimes moving together.

Coordination fragmentation occurs when a shared structure still exists formally but can no longer keep local realities sufficiently connected. Teams, groups, or roles develop their own information, rules, meanings, and objectives, and the translation cost among them grows. Each local unit may be effective on its own while the larger system becomes unable to recombine those local actions. The problem is not necessarily unwillingness to cooperate; the shared interface may no longer be capable of carrying difference.

As fragmentation persists, legitimacy begins to weaken. Coordination legitimacy here is not a partisan or ideological judgment. It means whether participants still regard the shared arrangement as sufficiently acceptable to justify its cost. If rules increasingly fail to serve shared goals, costs repeatedly fall on positions that cannot influence the rule, or exceptions remain open only to a stable minority, participants can continue formal compliance while withdrawing genuine commitment.

Legitimacy erosion is dangerous because formal structure can survive longer than trust. Institutions, meetings, and procedures can remain while participants shift toward private protection, informal networks, and local bargaining because they no longer expect formal coordination to treat reality credibly. The shared structure then loses visibility into actual behavior. The more people route around it, the less accurately it reads the system; the less accurately it reads, the more its decisions diverge from reality.

In that environment, coordination becomes vulnerable to capture. Resources, rules, information, and power that were designed to serve shared operation can gradually be used in stable ways that favor a local interest. Capture does not require a conspiracy. It can emerge through persistent information advantage, control of entry points, specialized knowledge, or rule complexity. Some positions simply become better able than others to make the common structure produce outcomes for them.

When captured coordination continues asking everyone to carry common cost while mainly protecting a narrow set of interests, legitimacy erodes further and fragmentation accelerates. Some groups build substitutes, some participants exit, and some cooperate only minimally. Attempts to preserve surface unity through additional force or procedural burden can increase execution cost without restoring shared acceptance. The problem is no longer one bad rule; it is a loss of confidence that participants still inhabit one governable reality.

Coordination collapse occurs when the shared layer can no longer keep multiple runtimes operating together. Resource allocation loses a credible path, information cannot cross local boundaries, conflict cannot be processed collectively, and decisions lack enough execution. Collapse does not require every local activity to stop. Some local runtimes may continue or even become stronger. What disappears is the former common layer that organized them as one continuing reality.

Repair is therefore cheaper earlier in the sequence. Fragmented interfaces, legitimacy signals, and capture risks should be addressed before collapse. Mature governance reconnects rule outcomes to shared goals, gives affected positions meaningful feedback and correction paths, prevents information and authority from remaining permanently closed, and allows the shared structure itself to be reviewed. The goal is not to preserve a particular form, but to preserve a structure that multiple realities can still reasonably accept as common.

blocks.label: Key judgment
blocks.text: Coordination failure often progresses through fragmentation, legitimacy erosion, capture, and collapse. Governance protects the ability of a shared structure to connect local realities, remain acceptable, and continue serving common operation rather than merely preserving its formal shape.

blocks.label: Reality Question
blocks.text: Look at a shared structure that is losing commonality. Is the earliest active problem fragmentation between local realities, declining legitimacy, or stable capture of resources and authority? If repair began now, which interface would need to change first?
